desc:
Count the start indices i for which the window text[i..i+m-1] (where m = |pattern|) differs from pattern in at most one position. An exact match counts as well.

Example: text = "abcabd", pattern = "abc". The windows are "abc" (0 differences), "bca" (3), "cab" (3) and "abd" (1), so the answer is 2. If pattern is longer than text, the answer is 0.
constraints: Both strings consist of lowercase English letters
hints: Comparing each window with the pattern takes O(n · m). Think about what a window with at most one mismatch looks like: a matching prefix, one wrong character, then a matching suffix.
For every window compute pre = the length of the longest common prefix of the window and the pattern. Z-function of pattern + '#' + text gives this for all windows at once.
Do the same on the reversed strings to get suf = the longest common suffix of the window and the pattern. The window has at most one mismatch exactly when pre + suf ≥ m - 1.
editorial: Let pre[i] be the length of the longest common prefix of pattern and text[i..], capped at m, and suf[i] the length of the longest common suffix of pattern and text[..i+m-1]. Both come from Z-functions: pre from pattern + '#' + text and suf from the same construction on the reversed strings.

If pre[i] = m the window is an exact match. Otherwise the first mismatch is at offset pre[i], and the window is acceptable exactly when everything after that offset matches, that is, when the common suffix covers the remaining m - pre[i] - 1 characters: suf[i] ≥ m - pre[i] - 1. This is equivalent to the single test pre[i] + suf[i] ≥ m - 1 which is also true for exact matches.

Two linear Z-function passes and one scan give O(n + m) time and space. The idea generalises to k mismatches by repeating 'jump over the next common prefix' k times, using a data structure for longest-common-extension queries.
